description: Time de estudantes de Eng. De Software de diferentes instituiçoes focados no desenvolvimento de um projeto afim de testar e desafiar ambas capacidades de desenvolver software com habilidades distintas.
summary: FirePoints is a web app that merges 26 years of NASA satellite fire detections over Brazil into one consistent record and turns it into a burning-activity calendar. MODIS (2000–) and VIIRS (2012–) cannot be compared directly: VIIRS sees about 3.8× more hotspots, which creates a false jump in 2012. We convert MODIS counts to the VIIRS scale with a factor for each biome and month, calibrated on 2012–2019 and validated year by year (0.9% mean error for Brazil). Users pick a state, a biome or draw their own area to see when it burns, how this season compares with the historical normal, where the fires concentrate, and to download the data. Early-warning teams, scientists and land managers get a single long record to anticipate critical periods and spot unusual seasons.
details:
What it does FirePoints answers four questions for any area of Brazil, from November 2000 to October 2026:

  1. When does it burn, and how much? A month-by-year calendar of active-fire detections, colored by intensity or by anomaly.
  2. Is this fire season normal? Each month is compared with its 2003–2025 mean (for example, "+37% above normal"), with a 10th–90th percentile band.
  3. Where does it burn? An interactive map with small pixels (0.025°, ≈2.8 km) over a dark basemap, with state boundaries and city names; a click reads the 0.1° cell (≈11 km) behind every number.
  4. Can two satellites be read as one record? A chart showing MODIS × factor against observed VIIRS for the selected area. Users choose a state (27), a biome (6), a region (5) or draw an area on the map, pick a period and download three CSVs: monthly series, per-cell counts, and the individual fire detections. The interface is available in English and Portuguese.

How it works

  • Data: NASA FIRMS MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra + Aqua, 1 km) and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m, both for Brazil; standard archive for the history, near-real-time only after the archive ends, so nothing is counted twice.
  • Cleaning: vegetation fires only (type = 0), MODIS confidence ≥ 30, VIIRS nominal/high confidence, dates converted to local time (America/Sao_Paulo), each detection assigned to a 0.1° cell. Result: 9.5 million MODIS and 17.9 million VIIRS detections.
  • Harmonization: the VIIRS/MODIS ratio changes by season (2.8 in April to 4.2 in October) and by biome (3.0 Cerrado to 4.5 Caatinga), so one global factor would bias both. We compute a factor k for each biome and calendar month over Feb 2012 – Dec 2019, when both sensors overlap and the MODIS orbits were still stable. Before Feb 2012 the series is MODIS × k; from then on it is observed VIIRS.
  • Validation: leaving each year of 2012–2019 out, the predicted national total differs from observed VIIRS by 0.9% on average (1.3% Amazônia to 7.4% Pampa). Regional factors cut the local error at 1° cells from 12.6% to 7.7% compared with one national factor. Applying the factors forward (2020–2025) fails as the MODIS orbits drift, so we only apply them backward.
  • Transparency: every month is labelled observed (VIIRS), estimated (2003 – Jan 2012) or partial (Nov 2000 – 2002, when only Terra flew).

Benefits A single, comparable 26-year record instead of two incompatible ones; anomalies that show whether a season is out of the ordinary; any custom area, not only predefined regions; open data and MIT-licensed code that anyone can rerun. The same method can bridge VIIRS S-NPP to NOAA-20/21 when S-NPP ends.

What we hope to achieve Give fire managers and early-warning teams a quick way to see a region's critical months and unusual seasons, and offer researchers a harmonized series ready to download.

Next step: fire outlooks A harmonized record is what a seasonal fire outlook needs for training. In a first test (forecasts issued every month from 2016 to 2025, each using only past data), adding the recent anomaly to the monthly normal cut Brazil's error for the next 1–3 months from 34% to 29%, with no gain further ahead. Our next step is to add climate drivers known in advance — lagged fire-weather indices from NASA's GFWED and ENSO forecasts — and show an outlook in the app only if it beats the normal in this same test.

Tools Python (pandas, NumPy, GeoPandas, Shapely, PyArrow, DuckDB), Streamlit (deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud), Plotly for charts, Folium (Leaflet) with Esri's Dark Gray Canvas basemap for the map, GitHub for code and the team's decision log.

Limitations These are hotspot detections, not fire events or burned area. Clouds and overpass times are not modelled. The Pampa has few detections and the largest error. 2000–2002 is under-counted and flagged as partial. The VIIRS S-NPP record in FIRMS ends on 2 Nov 2026.
